results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 68 body units' summaries match the controlling idea of their aligned spec paragraph, in spec order (p01-p66); the five opening callouts are not spec paragraphs and match none. No unit is missing, extra or out of order.

Only Scene ¶4 was marked (ring and losses / detection worked but held nothing). The ring's facts are the incident the paragraph is about and the evidence for its single point, stated in 'The media part of the review is uncomfortable because detection worked'; this matches p08's controlling idea. No other unit needed two summaries.

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: intro and concepts to S1; pipeline to S2 (doors, stages, timing) and S1 (provenance, documents); privacy to S3; derivatives and lifecycle to S4; hashing to S5; understanding and rich media to S1 (MediaReady, one model with profiles); in-practice, trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, CA view and questions apply S1-S5; conclusion synthesizes S4 and S5.

Each figure caption states what it shows; each table is introduced by a sentence stating what it sets out and followed by interpretation (pipeline table by the gate, document and blocking-timing paragraphs; retention table by deletion and hash-retention paragraphs; cost table by the processing-line paragraph; vertical table by the jobs-column paragraph). Each source and statistic is followed by its consequence (e.g. 'which shows automated gallery ordering running at scale', 'At that volume, reading text in images is worth running in-house', 'That one field is the difference...').

Every section and paragraph boundary expresses its declared relationship and picks up the declared known information (e.g. 'Answering Ingrid's question needs precise words', 'The sanitize stage exists because', 'Hearthly's bill comes next', 'Derivatives can be regenerated; masters cannot', 'Hashing compares photos with each other; image models read each photo', 'Several failures above trace to', 'The Lyon apartment shows the other side ... The same signal that blocks a scam supports a legitimate merge'). No failing boundary.

results.quote: A third finding, from Tradeyard, is already on her list: the stored originals of Femke's bike photos still carry the GPS coordinates of her home.
results.finding: Both readers lost count: a 'third' finding is numbered and described before the first of the two announced documents, so 'The first is the media bill' then reads against three items (A: 'for a moment I lost count of the two documents'; B: 'made me re-read'). Femke herself is book cast from meet-veldmark, so the name is not the problem; the ordinal and placement wording are. The spec only requires the finding to be on Ingrid's list here; the prose can mark it as separate from Julien's two documents without numbering it ahead of them.

The introduction opens with an intriguing example (marketplaces as image businesses measured in bytes) bridged from the attribute dictionary, then the staged-pipeline problem, the one-contract claim and a roadmap; none of the weak patterns.

The conclusion does not open with 'in conclusion', adds no new idea or evidence, and does not end on a restated thesis: it synthesizes the two documents into one failure and one contract, then hands off to location-and-geo as declared.

States what no single section states ('Julien's two documents describe one failure ... One contract answers both', crediting SHA-256 and PDQ on the way in and on-demand derivatives and lifecycle after it) and why it matters ('Sharing the contract and the index first is cheap, cuts the bill and stops fraud earlier, without waiting for storage to move').
Returns to Julien's two documents from the scene and answers Ingrid's question with one contract rather than separate projects, as callback.to declares.

Both cold readers predicted the sections in the declared order (the two Veldmark documents; terms; pipeline and publication checks; what photos reveal as privacy; the bill's half of derivatives/CDN then storage tiers and lifecycle; the ring's half of perceptual hashing; image understanding beyond fraud; video, tours and floor plans; public examples, Hearthly's plan in numbers, trade-offs, verticals, failure modes, Chief Architect's view, review questions) and the evidence (the fictional Veldmark case with numbers, public examples from real marketplaces). Gaps are minor: neither names standards as an evidence type, and the reader-intro notes the IN THIS CHAPTER callout groups 'hashing and classification' where the roadmap separates them.

The reader names all expected elements: the match only created a 'possible duplicate' queue item while the listing went live; it returned a distance with no relationship between the sellers; the index covered one brand. Fix: for rentals (high-risk), a PDQ match to a different seller or a block-listed hash holds the listing for the trust decision within the publication budget, each match carries the seller relationship, and the index is shared group-wide.

The reader names the three causes (feed re-downloads stored as byte-identical copies, nine stored renditions kept as long as the original, ended listings' media never deleted) and the fixes: SHA-256 content addressing with change-aware fetching (media change date, conditional requests, hash comparison); on-demand derivatives behind a CDN in AVIF/WebP with bounded widths; lifecycle by listing state to Coldline/Archive with minimum storage durations, deleted by retention class.

The reader answers no, because the stored originals keep GPS and one misconfigured bucket exposes them; strip in sanitization before the master is written; do not keep raw originals without a documented purpose, with restricted access and short retention; purge derivatives from the CDN on deletion.
